segments.title: Why Wikipedia is not stable citable evidence
segments.summary: Historians do use Wikipedia, but its changing text and lack of one accountable author make it unsuitable as stable evidence for a citation.
segments.question: Why do historians avoid citing Wikipedia even though they use it?
segments.answerShort: Wikipedia pages lack a single accountable author and can change after a researcher reads them, so another scholar may not be able to return to the same evidence.
segments.body: A citation should let another reader return to the same evidence and assess the person or work responsible for it. Dr. Clarke argues that a Wikipedia entry lacks a single author who can be held accountable for an error. Its editable nature is a double-edged feature: it can be current, but it can also be altered by bad actors or change after a researcher has read it. That makes it difficult to cite as a fixed source. His point connects historical method to reproducibility, since another scholar should be able to retrace the research and reach a comparable result.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that Wikipedia lacks one accountable author and can change after it has been consulted.

segments.title: Wikipedia as a research starting point
segments.summary: On an unfamiliar subject, historians can use Wikipedia to find cited works and then follow those works' own bibliographies and sources.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke explains how Wikipedia can support the beginning of a research process. On an unfamiliar subject, he looks at the sources listed at the bottom of a page. He then checks those works and follows their bibliographies and source lists outward, building a broader body of evidence. This makes Wikipedia a signpost toward citable material rather than the authority on which the final claim rests. He also notes that he uses it to find images for explanatory videos.

evidence.note: The transcript explains using Wikipedia to find sources, follow bibliographies, and locate images.

segments.title: Citation styles and the flow of an argument
segments.summary: Harvard, Chicago, and Vancouver all identify sources, but footnotes or endnotes can keep citations from interrupting historical prose.
segments.question: Why do historians often prefer Chicago or Vancouver citation styles?
segments.answerShort: Their footnotes or endnotes preserve the flow of an argument while still allowing readers to trace its sources.
segments.body: The video compares Harvard's parenthetical in-text citations with Chicago-style footnotes and Vancouver-style endnotes. Dr. Clarke sees the systems as serving the same basic purpose while placing the reference in different locations. He argues that historians often prefer notes because repeated brackets can break the flow of an analytical case. Footnotes keep a source readily available to readers, while endnotes can be easier for publishers to place in print. The choice is therefore partly about scholarly transparency and partly about the readability and production of an argument.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Harvard, Chicago, and Vancouver and explains note placement.
